answer_text:
Interpreting “preserves matrix multiplication” as
\[
f(AB)=f(A)f(B)\qquad\text{for all }A,B\in M_n(\mathbb C),
\]
let \(f(A)=\operatorname{tr}(XA)\).

Let \(E_{ij}\) denote the matrix units, and put \(\lambda=f(I)\). Then
\[
\lambda=f(I)=f(I^2)=f(I)^2=\lambda^2,
\]
so \(\lambda\in\{0,1\}\).

### Case 1: \(\lambda=0\)
For every \(A\),
\[
f(A)=f(AI)=f(A)f(I)=f(A)\cdot 0=0.
\]
Thus \(f\equiv 0\). Since the trace pairing is nondegenerate,
\[
\operatorname{tr}(XA)=0\ \forall A \implies X=0.
\]
So \(X=0\) always gives a valid solution.

### Case 2: \(\lambda=1\) and \(n\ge 2\)
Let
\[
\alpha_i=f(E_{ii}).
\]
Since \(E_{ii}^2=E_{ii}\),
\[
\alpha_i=\alpha_i^2,
\]
so \(\alpha_i\in\{0,1\}\). Also, for \(i\neq j\),
\[
E_{ii}E_{jj}=0,
\]
so
\[
\alpha_i\alpha_j=f(E_{ii}E_{jj})=0.
\]
But
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i=f(I)=1.
\]
Hence exactly one diagonal value is \(1\). Say
\[
f(E_{pp})=1,\qquad f(E_{ii})=0\ (i\neq p).
\]

Choose \(q\neq p\). Then
\[
E_{pq}E_{qq}=E_{pq},
\]
so
\[
f(E_{pq})=f(E_{pq}E_{qq})=f(E_{pq})f(E_{qq})=0.
\]
Similarly,
\[
f(E_{qp})=f(E_{qq}E_{qp})=f(E_{qq})f(E_{qp})=0.
\]
But
\[
E_{pq}E_{qp}=E_{pp},
\]
so
\[
1=f(E_{pp})=f(E_{pq}E_{qp})=f(E_{pq})f(E_{qp})=0,
\]
a contradiction. Therefore no such nonzero \(f\) exists when \(n\ge 2\).

### Case \(n=1\)
Here \(M_1(\mathbb C)=\mathbb C\). If \(X=[x]\), then
\[
f(A)=xA.
\]
Multiplicativity gives
\[
xAB=(xA)(xB)=x^2AB
\]
for all \(A,B\in\mathbb C\), so \(x^2=x\). Hence \(x=0\) or \(x=1\).

Thus the complete answer is
\[
\boxed{
\begin{cases}
X=0, & n\ge 2,\\[2mm]
X=0\ \text{or}\ X=I_1, & n=1.
\end{cases}
}
\]

In particular, if one only asks for a single matrix \(X\) that works for every \(n\), then
\[
\boxed{X=0}.
\]
